title: Taste and see (Psalm 34)
hookLine: O taste and see that the Lord is good
carry: near the brokenhearted, not the strong

cards: You can read a whole cookbook about peaches: their varieties, their season, the chemistry of their sugars. You can become an expert.
Then someone hands you a real one, warm from the tree, and you bite into it, and the juice runs down your wrist, and in two seconds you know something the whole book couldn't tell you.
Some knowledge only comes through the mouth. One psalm turns that ordinary truth into an invitation, and it's been sung in churches for more than sixteen hundred years at one particular moment.

teach.b: Psalm thirty-four, in the King James Bible: "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him." Taste first, then see. Not see first, and maybe taste later if the evidence is good enough.
The psalm puts experience before understanding: you come to know God's goodness the way you know a peach, by trying it. And this isn't a psalm of easy times.
The heading ties it to David running for his life, pretending to be mad in front of a foreign king so he'd be let go. The heading names the king Abimelech, while the book of Samuel calls him Achish.
Scholars have different explanations; the sources don't settle it.

teach.h: A SONG OF A NARROW ESCAPE.
teach.b: Either way, this is a song from someone who escaped by the skin of his teeth. "I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears."
And one of its best-known lines: "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." Near the brokenhearted. Not the strong.
The psalm is also an acrostic: in Hebrew, its verses run roughly through the alphabet, one letter after another, like a child's ABC of trust. And here's where the taste comes in for many Christians.
In the fourth century, Cyril of Jerusalem described the newly baptized hearing a singer chant this verse as they came forward to receive communion: taste and see.

teach.h: O TASTE AND SEE THAT THE LORD IS GOOD.
teach.b: Many churches still sing it at the Lord's table.

how: Many churches, Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican and others, sing 'O taste and see' during communion, a custom described as early as Cyril of Jerusalem in the fourth century.

games.q: you're David, captured in a foreign king's court, and in danger. what does the story say you do?
o: pretend to be mad, so they let you go.
games.why: he acts mad, and is driven away. Psalm 34 is the song of that narrow escape: I sought the LORD, and he heard me.

practice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, take one small bite or sip; if not, save this for your next meal. Don't chew yet: notice the texture and the temperature, then chew slowly and let the flavor arrive, change and fade.
If you pray, give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Acrostic. A poem built so its verses run through the alphabet, one letter at a time, like this psalm of tasting God's goodness.
